Note the three cited percentages are intertextuality/fourth-wall features, not temporal ones, despite the claim's 'temporal complexity' label.

claim: Narrative-level features still identify AI fiction at 93.9% macro-F1 after professional-style rewriting, so surface edits do not humanize structure.
source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)
quote: far harder to humanize

verdict.trueWording: far harder to "humanize"
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the Introduction (with 'humanize' in scare quotes). §4.2 confirms 93.9% macro-F1 on style-edited stories vs 95.5% unedited, a 1.6-point drop. One precision caveat: the rewriting is LAMP span-level artifact removal performed by Gemini itself using 25 few-shot examples from professional writers on 278 Gemini stories — not rewriting by professionals, so 'professional-style rewriting' is a loose gloss.

claim: LLM-processed text shows abrupt excess of style words such as delves (28x), showcasing (10x), intricate, underscores, pivotal, meticulously, realm; 2024 excess words were 66% verbs and 16% adjectives.
source: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát & Lause (arXiv 2406.07016; Science Advances 2025)

verdict.trueWording: delves (r=28.0), showcasing (r=10.2), underscores (r=10.9); 66% verbs, 16% adjectives
verdict.note: No quote supplied. Kobak et al. give delves r=28.0 and showcasing r=10.2 exactly, and 'hundreds of words have abruptly increased their frequency after ChatGPT became available'. The POS split is real but narrower than stated: 'Out of all 319 excess style words in 2024, 66% were verbs and 16% were adjectives' — style words, not all excess words. 'intricate' is the paper's own example of a style word; 'pivotal', 'realm' and 'meticulously' appear in the paper only as words identified by cited work (Liang et al. 2024b; Gray 2024) and in illustrative AI-style sentences, not in Kobak's own headline excess list.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the 66%-verbs/16%-adjectives split holds only of the 319 excess STYLE words, and pivotal, realm and meticulously are not in Kobak's own excess list.

claim: Instruction-tuned LLMs use nominalizations 1.5–2x, 'that' subject clauses 2.6x and phrasal coordination 1.9x human rates, producing a noun-heavy academic style regardless of genre.
source: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025
quote: informationally dense, noun-heavy style

verdict.trueWording: "informationally dense, noun-heavy style"
verdict.note: Quote appears verbatim twice. Figures confirmed: nominalizations 'at 1.5 to 2 times the rate of humans' generally, and for GPT-4o specifically ''that' clauses as subject 2.6 times as often (d=0.77), nominalizations 2.1 times as often (d=1.23), and phrasal coordination 1.9 times as often (d=0.81)'. Two glosses: the 2.6x and 1.9x figures are GPT-4o-specific, not all instruction-tuned models; and 'academic' is the claim's word, not the paper's, though the paper does attribute the style to instruction tuning across a diverse array of genres.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the 2.6x "that"-clause and 1.9x phrasal-coordination rates are GPT-4o-specific, not all instruction-tuned models, and "academic" is not the paper's word.

claim: LLM prose repeats templates such as 'sense of', 'weight of', 'mix of', and the word 'unspoken' appears in about 15% of LLM outputs but rarely in human samples.
source: Chakrabarty, Laban & Wu (CHI 2025)

verdict.note: No quote supplied, but both halves are explicit in Section 5.3: 'Figure 6 shows how a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses. Similarly phrases such as weight of, sense of, mix of occur very rarely or not at all in original seed paragraphs... while they occur frequently in LLM-generated responses.' One imprecision: the paper reserves 'syntactic templates' for its part-of-speech n-gram analysis (Table 8) and files these three phrases under recurrent awkward words/phrases; the claim merges the two.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "templates" — the paper files "sense of / weight of / mix of" under recurrent awkward words and phrases, reserving "syntactic templates" for its POS n-gram analysis.

claim: LLM stories show 7–9x higher 'drop ratios' than human stories, meaning a suspenseful element is resolved immediately after it peaks instead of being developed.
source: Xu et al., Echoes in AI (PNAS 2025)

verdict.trueWording: "LLM-generated stories lead to 7–9 higher drop ratio than human-written ones"
verdict.note: No quote supplied. Figure confirmed in Section 5 (the page literally reads '7–9 higher drop ratio', the multiplication sign apparently lost in the HTML build). Mechanism supported: 'a high drop ratio indicates that the Sui Generis score decreases immediately after the peak at position i, without progressively unraveling the surprising plot,' associated with 'abrupt resolutions that leave key suspenseful plot elements unresolved.' Slight tension in the claim's gloss: the paper's drop measures a surprising element being dropped or hastily closed off, sometimes left unresolved, rather than strictly 'resolved'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "resolved immediately after it peaks" — the paper's drop measures an element dropped or hastily closed off, sometimes left unresolved, not strictly resolved.

claim: Major Setback and Climax arrive about 10–15% earlier in GPT-4 narratives, and human stories sustain higher suspense with the gap widening from midpoint to end.
source: Tian et al. (EMNLP 2024)
quote: higher levels of suspense

verdict.trueWording: "a substantial advancement (i.e., early occurrence) of TP4 and TP5"
verdict.note: The quote 'higher levels of suspense' IS verbatim ('human-written stories consistently exhibit higher levels of suspense'), as is the widening gap ('the gap begins to enlarge as the plot progresses from the midpoint (0.5 relative position) towards the end'). Downgraded from VERBATIM because the claim's magnitude is unsourced: the strings '10%' and '15%' appear nowhere in the paper, and the earlier arrival of Major Setback (TP4) and Climax (TP5) is reported only qualitatively plus a violin plot (Figure 2) with no numeric positions. The '10–15% earlier' figure appears to be eyeballed from that figure.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "about 10–15% earlier" — the strings 10% and 15% appear nowhere in the paper; the advancement of TP4/TP5 is reported only qualitatively and in a violin plot.

claim: LLM story character networks are denser (0.338–0.470 vs 0.182), more positive (mean edge weight 0.236–0.659 vs −0.061) and more clustered than human science-fiction, with far less variability.
source: Nonaka & Perry (arXiv 2510.18932, Sep 2025)
quote: less conflict-driven social dynamics

verdict.trueWording: less conflict-driven social dynamics
verdict.note: arXiv 2510.18932v1, Nonaka & Perry. Quote verbatim. Table 1 in the raw HTML confirms density 0.338–0.470 vs human 0.182, clustering 0.623–0.766 vs 0.485, human mean edge weight −0.061 ('the only negative average edge weight'). ONE CORRECTION: the LLM edge-weight range is 0.235–0.659 (GPT-4o Mini = 0.235), not 0.236–0.659. Human corpus is confirmed science fiction (Project Gutenberg, genre-filtered, n=168). 'Far less variability' is supported by the paper's framing — 'LLMs have connectivity measure scores that cluster closely, while human-written stories are dispersed' — though per-metric SDs are mixed (human density SD 0.056 is actually lower than every model's).
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the LLM edge-weight floor is 0.235 (GPT-4o Mini), not 0.236, and "far less variability" is not borne out per-metric — human density SD (0.056) is lower than every model's.

claim: LLMs produce mood-laden 'perceived space' at about twice the human rate (GPT-4.1 0.47 vs human 0.19) and under-produce action space, substituting atmosphere for embodied movement.
source: Rohrbacher et al., How LLMs Build Fictional Worlds (arXiv 2609.02482, Sep 2026)
quote: roughly twice the human baseline

verdict.trueWording: roughly twice the human baseline
verdict.note: arXiv 2609.02482v1, Rohrbacher, Nieth, Salin, Eskofier & Mahlberg. Verbatim: 'Whereas human-authored fiction shows normalized frequencies of around 0.19 in both languages, all four models exceed this level, with GPT 4.1 reaching around 0.47 in English and 0.38 in German, roughly twice the human baseline.' CAVEAT on the second half: the action-space deficit is not universal — 'GPT 4.1 is the only model that remains close to or above the human baseline'; Gemma 3, Mistral 3.2 and LlaMA 3.3 fall below it. The abstract's own framing does support the substitution claim: humans 'predominantly employ action space ... whereas LLMs systematically overproduce perceived space, emphasizing atmosphere and affect.'

verdict.note: arXiv 2407.01119v2, Marco, Gonzalo, Mateo & Ramón del Castillo. Quote verbatim ('In all dimensions, GPT-4 receives predominantly scores of 0/1, while Pron receives mostly 2/3.'). claim: On an epic-comedy task GPT-4 outscored five human writers overall (80.2 vs 70.1) and on epic-genre habitation (8.1 vs 4.9); humans led only on originality (8.0 vs 7.6) with humor near-tied (6.4 vs 6.0).
source: Gómez-Rodríguez & Williams, A Confederacy of Models (Findings EMNLP 2023)
quote: Humans retain an edge in creativity

verdict.trueWording: Humans retain an edge in creativity
verdict.note: Quote is word for word in the abstract on the ACL Anthology landing page. That page carries the abstract only — none of the numbers are on it — so I additionally pulled the paper PDF (aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.966.pdf), Table 2, which confirms every figure: chatgpt-gpt4 overall 80.2±7.3 vs human 70.1±17.4; item 7 (epic-genre habitation) 8.1±1.4 vs 4.9±2.1; item 5 (creativity/originality) human 8.0±2 vs 7.6±1; item 10 (dark humor) human 6.4±3.4 vs 6.0±2.8. One imprecision: humans also edged GPT-4 on humor (6.4 vs 6.0), so 'led only on originality' is not strictly true, though the claim itself calls humor near-tied.

claim: LLM text carries more joy and positive emotion while humans show more fear and disgust; LLMs also use more pronouns and magnify male-pronoun bias.

verdict.note: No quotation supplied. claim: In blind evaluation by 20+ professional TV screenwriters, direct LLM screenwriting showed lack of thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue and thin character development, mimicking screenplay style without conciseness or visual language.
source: Lei, Zong, Li, Zhou & Liu, Beyond Direct Generation (arXiv 2510.23163, Oct 2025)
quote: lack of thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue, and insufficient character development

verdict.trueWording: preliminary end-to-end experiments revealed these shortcomings, say the authors
verdict.note: MISATTRIBUTION. The quoted string is verbatim on the page, but it describes the AUTHORS' OWN preliminary experiments: 'Our preliminary experiments with this end-to-end approach revealed suboptimal results. The generated screenplays often suffer from a lack of thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue, and insufficient character development.' The blind evaluation by 'over 20 experienced screenwriters' (professional Chinese television drama screenwriters) produced the Expert Score / 75% win rate, not this defect list. 'Mimicking screenplay style without conciseness or visual language' is also the authors' intro framing: 'outputs that superficially mimic screenplay style but lack the conciseness, visual language, and structural integrity'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the defect list is misattributed — thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue and thin character development come from the authors' own preliminary experiments, not from the blind screenwriter evaluation.
